question: to the Commission Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE), Isabella Lövin (Verts/ALE), Pär Holmgren (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Mining projects in the pipeline in Medelpad and Jämtland – including the extraction of alum shale containing uranium, vanadium, zinc, nickel and molybdenum in Oviken, as well as lithium mining near the river Indalsälven at Järkvissle – pose a risk to the water systems that supply drinking water to around 37 000 inhabitants of Sundsvall and Timrå. The local water authority Mittsverige Vatten has expressed serious concerns about long-term water quality. Since 2024, the Commission has been pursuing an infringement procedure (INFR(2024)2236) against Sweden regarding the country’s failure to properly implement the EU Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC). Through its RESourceEU action plan, among other schemes, the Commission is also pushing for more mining in the EU, as well as faster permitting processes. With that in mind: 1.

Given the ongoing infringement procedure, is the Commission confident that Sweden is correctly implementing the Water Framework Directive and the EU rules on the quality of drinking water when it comes to new mining operations?
Does the Commission take the view that it is in line with EU rules to grant mining permits when there is evidence of serious risks to drinking water quality?

How does the Commission intend to ensure – in forthcoming guidance documents, for example – that an increase in mining and streamlined permitting processes do not have a negative impact on the implementation of EU environment and water rules, and are not likely to have an adverse effect on EU citizens’ access to clean drinking water?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) The Commission opened an infringement case in 2024 against Sweden1 for failure to correctly transpose the Water Framework Directive (WFD)2 by not providing for periodic reviews of relevant controls and water permits. This infringement case is ongoing. It is not directly related to alleged shortcomings in the authorisation of new mining operations. The Commission is also in the process of assessing the transposition of the revised Drinking Water Directive (DWD)3 in all Member States. The process of granting mining permits must comply with, inter alia, the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive4, which ensures that any significant effects on water are integrated in the preparation and assessment of projects. An infringement case is ongoing against Sweden5 regarding incorrect transposition of that Directive. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law, including with regard to individual cases of potential breach of the water quality rules. This includes e.g. Article 4(7) WFD for new projects, Article 7(3) WFD for the protection of drinking water, as well as the DWD. The Commission has recently adopted guidance6 aiming to help reduce uncertainties regarding procedures and assessments during permitting of new or existing activities affecting water bodies, with a focus on the mining sector. The goal is to support Europe’s overall resilience, whilst keeping a high level of protection of the environment and human health.
